title: Stomach Pain After Drinking: Causes, Relief, and When to Worry
excerpt: Why your stomach hurts after drinking alcohol, what the location of the pain can mean, how to settle it the morning after, which painkillers to avoid, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why your stomach hurts after drinking, how to ease the pain the next morning, which painkillers to avoid, and the warning signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most stomach pain after drinking is your stomach lining reacting to alcohol. Alcohol irritates the lining directly, pushes up acid, and loosens the valve that keeps acid out of your food pipe. For a social drinker, that usually means a burning, gnawing, or crampy ache the next morning that settles within a day or so with water, bland food, and rest. A small number of cases are something more serious, mainly pancreatitis, a bleeding ulcer, or liver trouble, and those have warning signs you should know. This guide explains what's happening, how to calm your stomach, which painkillers to avoid, and exactly when the pain means you need a doctor.

**The quick rules:** Sip water, eat something plain like toast or rice, and use a simple antacid if the pain is burning. Skip ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen while your stomach hurts, because they can make an irritated lining worse. Don't drink more alcohol to "settle" it. And if the pain is severe, spreads to your back, comes with vomiting you can't stop, blood, black stools, or yellow skin or eyes, get medical care today rather than waiting it out.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room if** you have severe or worsening belly pain, pain that bores through to your back, vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, a rigid or very tender belly, fainting, a racing heart, or confusion. **See a doctor within a day or two if** the pain lasts more than 48 hours, keeps coming back every time you drink, wakes you at night, comes with yellowing skin or eyes or dark urine, or comes with weight loss or trouble swallowing. If you drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Please talk to a doctor rather than managing it alone.

## Why Does My Stomach Hurt After Drinking Alcohol?

Alcohol is hard on the whole digestive tract, but the stomach takes the first hit. Several things happen at once, and any one of them can cause pain.

### 1. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining (gastritis)

Your stomach is lined with a layer of mucus that protects it from its own acid. Alcohol, especially in stronger concentrations, damages that protective layer and the cells underneath it. Doctors call the resulting inflammation **gastritis**. After a single heavy night it's usually short-lived and is sometimes called acute or "erosive" gastritis, because the lining can develop small raw spots.

Gastritis pain is typically a burning or gnawing ache in the upper middle of your belly, just below the breastbone. It often comes with nausea, a sour taste, feeling full quickly, or bloating. It tends to be worse on an empty stomach, which is why it can feel brutal first thing in the morning.

### 2. Alcohol increases acid and causes reflux

Alcohol stimulates the stomach to produce acid, and research on gastric physiology suggests that fermented drinks like beer and wine tend to stimulate acid more than distilled spirits do. At the same time, alcohol relaxes the **lower esophageal sphincter**, the ring of muscle that acts as a valve between your stomach and your food pipe. With that valve loosened, acid splashes upward. The result is heartburn, a burning feeling in the chest or throat, sour burps, and sometimes a cough or hoarse voice in the morning.

Lying down soon after drinking, especially after a late, heavy meal, makes reflux much more likely.

### 3. Alcohol changes how your gut moves

Alcohol affects the muscles that move food through your gut. In the stomach it can slow emptying, so food and drink sit there longer, which adds to bloating and nausea. Further down, in the intestines, it tends to speed things up and interferes with how the gut absorbs water and salts. That's a big part of why many people get cramps and loose stools the morning after.

### 4. Alcohol makes the gut lining "leakier"

Research suggests alcohol can loosen the tight seals between the cells lining the intestine, temporarily making the gut wall more permeable. This is one of the ways heavy drinking is thought to drive inflammation in the body. In the short term, it may contribute to the general queasy, crampy, unwell feeling of a rough morning.

### 5. Dehydration and low blood sugar

Alcohol makes you urinate more, and if you also vomited or sweated, you can wake up quite dry. Dehydration on its own can cause cramping and nausea. Alcohol also interferes with the liver's ability to release sugar into the blood, so after a night of drinking without much food, low blood sugar can add shakiness, weakness, and nausea to stomach pain.

### 6. What you drank and ate with it

The alcohol itself isn't the only culprit. Common add-ons that upset the stomach include:

- **Carbonation** from beer, sparkling wine, and soda mixers, which adds gas and pressure.
- **Sugary mixers and cocktails**, which can pull water into the gut and cause cramps and diarrhea.
- **Acidic mixers** like citrus juice, and acidic drinks like many wines.
- **Caffeine** from energy-drink or cola mixers, which can add to reflux.
- **Greasy late-night food**, which slows stomach emptying and can trigger reflux or, in people with gallstones, a gallbladder attack.
- **Spicy food**, which can aggravate an already irritated lining.

If your stomach hurts after one particular drink but not others, the mixer or the carbonation is often the real problem.

## Where Does It Hurt? What the Location Can Tell You

Belly pain is hard to pin down, and location alone can't diagnose anything. Still, it gives useful clues about what's most likely going on.

### Upper middle stomach pain after drinking

This is the most common pattern. A burning or gnawing ache just under the breastbone usually points to **gastritis** or **reflux**. It's often worse when your stomach is empty and may ease a little after eating something bland or taking an antacid.

The important exception: severe, steady pain in the upper middle belly that **spreads through to your back**, gets worse after eating, and comes with vomiting can be **pancreatitis**. More on that below. This is not something to sleep off.

### Left side pain after drinking

The stomach sits mostly on the upper left side, so gastritis can feel left-sided. The pancreas also stretches across the upper belly toward the left. Mild, burning pain on the upper left that improves over a day is most often the stomach. Severe pain, especially with back pain or vomiting, needs a doctor to rule out pancreatitis. Lower left cramping that comes with diarrhea is usually the bowel reacting to alcohol.

### Right side pain after drinking

Your liver and gallbladder sit under the right ribs. A dull ache or fullness there after drinking can have many causes, but it shouldn't be ignored if it keeps happening. Sharp, cramping pain under the right ribs after a fatty meal, sometimes spreading to the right shoulder, is a classic pattern for a **gallbladder attack**. Pain under the right ribs together with yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pale stools can point to **liver inflammation** and needs prompt medical care.

### Lower belly cramps

Cramping lower down, with gas, bloating, or diarrhea, is usually the intestines reacting to alcohol, sugar, or carbonation. It tends to pass once things settle and you rehydrate. People with irritable bowel syndrome often find alcohol is a reliable trigger.

## Stomach Pain the Next Day: Is It Just a Hangover?

For most people, yes. Stomach pain, nausea, and diarrhea are standard hangover symptoms, alongside headache, fatigue, and thirst. They typically peak the morning after and fade over the course of the day as alcohol and its by-products clear and your stomach lining begins to recover. If nausea is your main problem, our [guide to hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) goes into more detail on settling a queasy stomach and keeping fluids down.

A few signs suggest it's more than a routine hangover:

- The pain is **getting worse** over the day instead of better.
- It's still there after **two days**.
- You **can't keep any fluids down** for many hours.
- The pain is **severe**, sharp, or focused in one spot.
- It happens **every time you drink**, even after small amounts.

Any of those is a reason to talk to a doctor rather than waiting for it to fade.

## How Long Does Stomach Pain After Drinking Last?

After a one-off heavy night, alcohol-related stomach irritation usually improves within a day and is often gone within two or three days, as long as you give your stomach a break from alcohol and irritating foods. The lining of the stomach renews itself quickly, which is why acute gastritis tends to settle on its own.

If you drink again before your stomach has recovered, the irritation can drag on. Pain that lasts more than a couple of days, or keeps returning, deserves a check-up. Ongoing gastritis can lead to ulcers or bleeding, and recurring pain can be a sign of something like chronic pancreatitis, an ulcer, or reflux disease that benefits from proper treatment.

## How to Stop Stomach Pain After Drinking

Here's what actually helps, roughly in order of what to do first.

### Rehydrate slowly

Take small, frequent sips of water rather than gulping a big glass, which can come right back up if you're nauseous. If you've had vomiting or diarrhea, an oral rehydration drink or an electrolyte drink helps replace lost salts. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) explains when they're worth it. Avoid more alcohol, strong coffee on an empty stomach, and fizzy drinks until you feel better.

### Eat something bland

A completely empty stomach often makes gastritis pain worse. Plain foods that are gentle on an irritated lining include:

- Toast, plain crackers, or rice
- Bananas
- Oatmeal
- Broth or a simple soup
- Plain eggs, if you can manage them

Leave greasy breakfasts, spicy food, citrus, and tomato-based dishes for another day. Eat small portions and see how you feel.

### Use an antacid or acid reducer for burning pain

For heartburn or a burning, gnawing ache, over-the-counter options can help:

- **Antacids** such as calcium carbonate (Tums and similar) neutralize acid quickly. Relief is fast but short-lived.
- **H2 blockers** such as famotidine reduce acid production for longer. They take a little longer to kick in.
- **Proton pump inhibitors** such as omeprazole are stronger acid reducers but are designed for regular use over days, not quick relief of a single bad morning.

Follow the label, and check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have kidney problems. If you find yourself needing acid medicine regularly after drinking, that's worth raising with a doctor.

**What about Pepto-Bismol?** It can help with nausea, indigestion, and diarrhea. Its active ingredient, bismuth subsalicylate, is a salicylate, a relative of aspirin, so it isn't a good fit for everyone. Our page on [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol) covers who should avoid it and how to use it safely.

### Be careful with painkillers

This is the most important point on the page for many people. **Ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen** (the NSAID painkillers) are hard on the stomach lining in their own right. They reduce the chemicals that help protect the lining, and their US labels carry a stomach bleeding warning for people who have three or more drinks a day. Taking them on top of alcohol-irritated gastritis can make pain worse and raises the risk of bleeding. Our page on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the risk in more detail.

**Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is gentler on the stomach, but it has its own issue: it's processed by the liver, and alcohol changes how the liver handles it. One standard dose after the alcohol has cleared is usually considered reasonable for healthy adults who don't drink heavily day to day, but never take more than the label allows. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers safe timing and limits.

If your main problem is stomach pain rather than a headache, you may not need a painkiller at all. Water, food, rest, and an antacid often do more.

### Try warmth and rest

A warm (not hot) heating pad on your belly can ease cramping. Rest with your head and upper body slightly raised if you have reflux, since lying flat lets acid creep up. Avoid tight waistbands, which press on a sore stomach.

### Don't drink "hair of the dog"

Another drink may numb things briefly, but it adds more alcohol to an already irritated lining and just delays recovery. Give your stomach at least a day or two off.

## Serious Causes You Shouldn't Ignore

Most stomach pain after drinking is minor. These are the less common causes that matter, because they need medical treatment.

### Acute pancreatitis

The pancreas is an organ behind the stomach that makes digestive enzymes. Heavy drinking is one of the most common causes of acute pancreatitis, along with gallstones. In pancreatitis, the pancreas becomes inflamed and its enzymes start irritating the organ itself.

Typical signs:

- Severe, steady pain in the upper belly, often spreading to the back
- Pain that gets worse after eating and may ease slightly when leaning forward
- Nausea and vomiting
- Fever, a fast heartbeat, or a swollen, tender belly

Pancreatitis can become life-threatening and is treated in hospital. It isn't limited to long-term heavy drinkers; a binge can trigger it in some people. If your pain fits this pattern, go to an emergency room.

### A bleeding ulcer or stomach bleeding

Alcohol isn't the main cause of stomach ulcers (that's usually the bacterium *H. pylori* or regular NSAID painkiller use), but it can irritate an existing ulcer and, combined with NSAIDs, raises the risk of bleeding. Warning signs include:

- Vomit with blood in it, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
- Black, sticky, tar-like stools
- Feeling faint, dizzy, or very pale

These are emergencies. Call 911 or go to an emergency room.

### A tear from forceful vomiting

Repeated, forceful vomiting or retching can cause a small tear where the food pipe meets the stomach, known as a Mallory-Weiss tear. It typically shows up as streaks of fresh red blood in vomit after a bout of heavy retching. Many of these heal on their own, but any blood in vomit should be checked by a doctor, because it can be hard to tell a small tear from something more serious.

### Liver inflammation

Pain or tenderness under the right ribs, especially with yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, a swollen belly, or unusual bruising, can be a sign of liver inflammation. This is more common in people who drink heavily over a long period, but it should always be checked. Our guide to [liver inflammation](/never-hungover/liver-inflammation-causes-symptoms-natural-treatment-2025) explains the warning signs in more detail.

### Alcoholic ketoacidosis

In people who drink a lot over several days while eating very little, and then vomit and can't keep food down, the body can build up acids in the blood. This causes belly pain, repeated vomiting, fast breathing, and feeling very unwell. It's uncommon in occasional social drinkers, but it's a medical emergency that needs hospital care.

### Gallbladder attacks

Gallstones aren't caused by alcohol, but a heavy, fatty late-night meal can trigger a gallbladder attack. Look for sharp, cramping pain under the right ribs or in the upper middle belly, sometimes spreading to the right shoulder blade, lasting from about half an hour to several hours. Repeated attacks, or pain with fever or yellowing skin, need medical attention.

## Why Does It Happen Every Time I Drink?

If your stomach hurts after almost every drink, even small amounts, it's worth looking for an underlying reason rather than accepting it. Common ones include:

- **Reflux disease (GERD)**, where acid reflux is a regular problem and alcohol reliably sets it off.
- **Chronic gastritis**, sometimes linked to *H. pylori* infection, which is treatable with antibiotics.
- **A stomach ulcer**, especially if you also take NSAID painkillers regularly.
- **Irritable bowel syndrome**, where alcohol is a common trigger for cramps and diarrhea.
- **A food intolerance** to something in the drink, such as gluten in beer for people with celiac disease, or a reaction to sulfites or histamine in wine.
- **Alcohol intolerance**, where the body breaks down alcohol poorly. This usually shows up as facial flushing, a stuffy nose, and a fast heartbeat, sometimes with nausea.

A doctor can test for some of these, such as *H. pylori*, and recommend treatment. That's far better than guessing, and many of these causes are very treatable.

## How to Prevent Stomach Pain After Drinking

The most reliable way to avoid alcohol-related stomach pain is to drink less, or not at all, on a given night. Beyond that, these habits help:

- **Eat a proper meal before you start.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches the lining and your bloodstream.
- **Alternate each drink with a glass of water.** It slows your pace and keeps you hydrated.
- **Choose drinks that agree with you.** If carbonation or sugary cocktails bother you, switch to still drinks or simpler mixers. Some people find spirits with a plain mixer easier than beer or wine; others find the opposite. Pay attention to your own pattern.
- **Go easy on late-night greasy food,** and avoid lying down right after eating.
- **Don't take ibuprofen or aspirin before or while drinking** to try to head off a hangover. You're stacking two stomach irritants.
- **Stop before you reach the point of vomiting.** Repeated vomiting is hard on the stomach and food pipe.

Our broader guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers pacing, food, and hydration in more depth.

## Does DHM Help With Stomach Pain After Drinking?

Honestly, there's no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin) soothes stomach pain or protects the stomach lining from alcohol in people. DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied mainly for how it may affect alcohol metabolism and liver health, and most of that research is in animals, with limited human data. It is not a treatment for gastritis, reflux, ulcers, or pancreatitis, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe for your stomach.

If you're interested in DHM for general hangover support, it's reasonable to try as part of a sensible plan that also includes food, water, and moderate drinking. Take it with food and water, since some people find any supplement on an empty stomach a little unsettling. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when. If you want to try DHM, a well-reviewed budget option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). If your stomach pain is severe or keeps coming back, please see a doctor rather than reaching for any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Stomach pain after drinking is common and usually comes from alcohol irritating your stomach lining, boosting acid, and triggering reflux. For a typical rough morning, the fix is simple: small sips of water, bland food, an antacid if it burns, rest, and a break from alcohol. Avoid ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen while your stomach is sore. Take it seriously if the pain is severe, spreads to your back, lasts more than two days, comes back every time you drink, or comes with blood, black stools, yellow skin, or vomiting you can't stop. Those signs need a doctor, and the most serious of them need an emergency room.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my stomach hurt after drinking alcohol?**

Alcohol irritates and inflames the stomach lining (gastritis), increases stomach acid, and relaxes the valve between your stomach and food pipe so acid can reflux upward. It also affects how your gut moves and absorbs water, which can cause cramps and diarrhea. Carbonation, sugary or acidic mixers, and greasy late-night food often add to the problem.

**How do I stop my stomach from hurting after drinking?**

Sip water slowly, eat something bland like toast, rice, or bananas, and use an antacid or famotidine for burning pain, following the label. Rest with your upper body slightly raised if you have heartburn. Avoid more alcohol, coffee on an empty stomach, spicy or greasy food, and NSAID painkillers like ibuprofen and aspirin until you feel better.

**How long does stomach pain after drinking last?**

After a single heavy night, stomach irritation usually improves within a day and is often gone in two to three days if you avoid alcohol and irritating foods. If the pain lasts longer than 48 hours, is getting worse, or returns every time you drink, see a doctor.

**Is it normal for your stomach to hurt the day after drinking?**

Mild stomach pain, nausea, and loose stools are common hangover symptoms and are usually not a cause for concern if they improve through the day. Severe pain, pain spreading to your back, vomiting you can't stop, blood in vomit, or black stools are not normal and need urgent medical care.

**What does pain on the left side after drinking mean?**

The stomach and part of the pancreas sit in the upper left belly, so mild burning on the left after drinking is most often gastritis. Severe or worsening pain on the upper left, especially if it spreads to your back or comes with vomiting, could be pancreatitis and needs prompt medical attention. Lower left cramping with diarrhea is usually the bowel reacting to alcohol.

**What does pain on the right side after drinking mean?**

The liver and gallbladder sit under the right ribs. A sharp, cramping pain there after a fatty meal can be a gallbladder attack. Pain under the right ribs together with yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pale stools can be a sign of liver inflammation. Recurring right-sided pain after drinking should be checked by a doctor.

**Can I take ibuprofen for stomach pain after drinking?**

It's best not to. Ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen can irritate the stomach lining and raise the risk of stomach bleeding, and their labels warn people who have three or more drinks a day. Alcohol has already irritated your stomach, so combining them can make pain worse. Antacids or acid reducers are a better fit for stomach pain, and acetaminophen is gentler on the stomach for headaches, within its label limits.

**When should I go to the ER for stomach pain after drinking?**

Go to an emergency room or call 911 for severe or worsening belly pain, pain that spreads to your back, vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, a rigid or very tender belly, fainting, a racing heart, confusion, or being unable to keep any fluids down for many hours.

**Does DHM help with stomach pain from alcohol?**

There's no good evidence that DHM soothes stomach pain or protects the stomach lining. It has been studied mainly for alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly in animals. It isn't a treatment for gastritis, reflux, or pancreatitis. For stomach pain, focus on water, bland food, antacids, and a break from alcohol, and see a doctor if the pain is severe or recurring.
